title: Niobe
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Niobe, whose husband's lyre built the walls of Thebes and who has borne seven sons and seven daughters, stops the Theban women in the middle of a rite for Latona and tells them to count her ancestry, her wealth and above all her children against a goddess who bore only two. Latona answers from the summit of Cynthus, and Apollo and Diana shoot the children down one after another, each by a different wound, while the boast turns into mourning and Amphion kills himself. Bereft at last, Niobe stiffens where she sits, is carried off by a whirlwind to her own country, and weeps there as marble still.
advisory: Niobe's fourteen children are shot down one after another, and for eleven lines together the poem stays with the wounds — a lung torn away on an arrow's barbs, an arrow driven through a throat as far as its feathers, blood jetting out of the hole — and Lectorium presents the passage unaltered, as Ovid wrote it.

sentences.t:
Lydia tota fremit, Phrygiaeque per oppida facti
rumor it et magnum sermonibus occupat orbem.
sentences.l: All Lydia is in an uproar, and through the towns of Phrygia the rumour of the deed goes, and it takes possession of the great world with talk.
sentences.i: All Lydia is buzzing with it; the story of what happened travels through the towns of Phrygia, and fills the whole wide world with talk.
sentences.n: The tale opens in mid-conversation: `facti`, "of the deed", is a genitive depending on `rumor`, and the deed is the one the previous tale ended on — Arachne's, named at line 150. `fremit` is the verb for the low growl of a crowd or a beast. `occupat orbem` is legal and military language, "seizes, takes possession of", so the gossip is imagined as taking the world the way an army takes a town.

sentences.t:
Ante suos Niobe thalamos cognoverat illam,
tum cum Maeoniam virgo Sipylumque colebat;
nec tamen admonita est poena popularis Arachnes
cedere caelitibus verbisque minoribus uti.
sentences.l: Before her own marriage Niobe had known her, at the time when as a girl she lived in Maeonia and on Sipylus; and yet she was not warned by the punishment of Arachne, her countrywoman, to yield to the heaven-dwellers and to use smaller words.
sentences.i: Niobe had known Arachne before her own marriage, back when she lived as a girl in Maeonia and on Sipylus; and even so, her countrywoman's punishment did not warn her to give way to the gods and to talk smaller.
sentences.n: `thalamos`, "bedchambers", stands for the marriage itself — a metonymy Ovid uses constantly. `popularis` is not "popular" but "of the same people": both women are Lydian, and the point is that Niobe had the warning close at hand. `admonita est ... cedere` — a passive verb of warning taking an infinitive; `uti` ("to use") takes the ablative, hence `verbis minoribus`. Sipylus, named here as her girlhood mountain, is where the tale will put her at the end.

sentences.t:
Multa dabant animos: sed enim nec coniugis artes
nec genus amborum magnique potentia regni
sic placuere illi, quamvis ea cuncta placerent,
ut sua progenies;
sentences.l: Many things gave her pride; but in fact neither her husband's arts nor the descent of them both nor the power of a great kingdom pleased her so — although all of it did please her — as her own offspring did;
sentences.i: Plenty gave her that pride; but in truth neither her husband's skill nor the descent of the pair of them nor the power of a great kingdom pleased her the way her own children did — though all of it pleased her well enough;
sentences.n: First sighting of a form you will meet on nearly every page: `placuere` is `placuerunt`, the poetic third-person plural perfect in `-ēre`. It is not a different tense, only a shorter ending. `coniugis artes` are Amphion's music (the walls he built with it come at line 178). `sed enim` is an idiom, "but the fact is", introducing the correction of what was just said.

sentences.t:
et felicissima matrum
dicta foret Niobe, si non sibi visa fuisset.
sentences.l: and Niobe would have been called the most fortunate of mothers, if she had not seemed so to herself.
sentences.n: `dicta foret` = `dicta esset`, pluperfect passive subjunctive in a past contrary-to-fact condition; `foret` for `esset` is ordinary in verse. The whole tale is folded into this sentence: what disqualified her was not being fortunate but knowing it. `felix` means both "fortunate" and "fruitful", and Niobe will take the word for herself out loud at line 193.

sentences.t:
Nam sata Tiresia venturi praescia Manto
per medias fuerat divino concita motu
vaticinata vias:
sentences.l: For Manto, born of Tiresias, foreknowing of what was to come, had prophesied through the middle of the streets, stirred by a divine impulse:
sentences.i: For Manto, the daughter of Tiresias, who knew what was coming, had gone prophesying down the middle of the streets, driven by the god's own impulse:
sentences.n: `sata Tiresia` — "sown from Tiresias", an ablative of origin, the standard poetic way of stating parentage; you will see it again at 185 and 221. `venturi praescia` — an adjective of knowing taking the genitive, with the future participle `venturi` used as a noun, "the thing about to come". `fuerat vaticinata` = `erat vaticinata`, the pluperfect of the deponent `vaticinor`, split across two lines with the prophecy itself in between.

sentences.t:
“Ismenides, ite frequentes
et date Latonae Latonigenisque duobus
cum prece tura pia lauroque innectite crinem.
sentences.l: "Women of Ismenus, go in throngs, and give incense to Latona and to the two born of Latona, with pious prayer, and twine your hair with laurel.
sentences.i: "Daughters of Thebes, go in crowds, and with dutiful prayer offer incense to Latona and Latona's two children, and twine laurel into your hair.
sentences.n: `Ismenides` are Theban women, named from the Ismenus, the river of Thebes; Ovid names Thebans by their landmarks throughout this book. `Latonigenis` — "Latona-born" — is one of the compound adjectives Latin verse builds freely out of a name plus `-gena` (compare `terrigena`, "earth-born", and `Troiugena`), and the two so described are Apollo and Diana. `cum prece ... pia` is what makes the incense an offering rather than smoke; `pius` is the whole Roman vocabulary of what is owed to gods, parents and the dead, and it will come back at line 250 in a very different scene.

sentences.t: Ore meo Latona iubet.”
sentences.l: By my mouth Latona commands."
sentences.i: "It is Latona who commands — through my mouth."
sentences.n: `ore meo` is an ablative of means, and the seer claims nothing of her own by it: she is the instrument, and the order belongs to the goddess. Four words end the speech, and the authority in them is what Niobe will contradict.

sentences.t:
Paretur, et omnes
Thebaides iussis sua tempora frondibus ornant
turaque dant sanctis et verba precantia flammis.
sentences.l: Obedience follows, and all the Theban women adorn their temples with the leaves that were ordered and give incense and praying words to the holy flames.
sentences.i: She is obeyed: every Theban woman dresses her brows with the leaves that were commanded, and gives incense and words of prayer to the holy flames.
sentences.n: `Paretur` is an impersonal passive — literally "it is being obeyed", with no subject at all. Latin does this freely with intransitive verbs that take a dative, and English has to invent someone to do the obeying. `iussis frondibus` is the laurel of the line before, now referred to only as "the ordered leaves". `tempora` here are the temples of the head, not time.

sentences.t:
Ecce venit comitum Niobe celeberrima turba,
vestibus intexto Phrygiis spectabilis auro,
et, quantum ira sinit, formosa:
sentences.l: Look — Niobe comes, most thronged about with a crowd of attendants, conspicuous for the gold woven into her Phrygian robes, and beautiful, as far as anger allows:
sentences.i: Look: here comes Niobe, at the centre of a great press of attendants, striking in her Phrygian robes with the gold woven through them — and beautiful, so far as anger lets her be:
sentences.n: `celeberrima` is not "most famous" here: `celeber` means "crowded, thronged", and the superlative goes with the ablative `turba`, "thronged with a crowd". `spectabilis` is "worth looking at", the word for a spectacle. The half-line `quantum ira sinit` is the sharpest thing in the passage: Ovid grants her beauty and takes part of it back in the same breath, and the anger is on her face before she has opened her mouth.

sentences.l: and moving, along with her graceful head, the hair let loose across each shoulder, she took her stand;
sentences.i: and with a toss of her lovely head that swung her loosened hair across both shoulders, she halted;
sentences.n: `inmissos ... capillos` — "sent down", i.e. unbound rather than dressed; Magnus's `inmissos` for `immissos` is the edition's spelling and is kept as printed. Note `umerum per utrumque`, with the preposition standing inside its own phrase instead of before it — anastrophe, very common in verse and worth learning to read past. The word order is deliberately tangled so that the hair sweeps across the line the way it sweeps across her shoulders.

sentences.t:
utque oculos circumtulit alta superbos,
“quis furor, auditos” inquit “praeponere visis
caelestes?
sentences.l: and when, standing tall, she had carried her proud eyes round about, "What madness," she says, "to set gods you have heard of before gods you see?
sentences.i: and when she had swept her proud eyes round the whole crowd, drawing herself up: "What madness is this — preferring gods you have only heard of to gods you can see?
sentences.n: The infinitive `praeponere` is the subject of the exclamation: "to prefer X to Y — what madness that is!" `auditos` and `visis` are participles used as nouns, "the heard ones" and "the seen ones", and the seen one she means is herself. `alta`, "tall", is a predicate adjective on the subject: she does the looking *tall*, and English needs a phrase where Latin needs one word. Watch the tenses shifting under you — `circumtulit` is perfect and `inquit` present, which is Ovid speeding up as the speech begins.

sentences.t:
aut cur colitur Latona per aras,
numen adhuc sine ture meum est?
sentences.l: Or why is Latona worshipped at altars, my godhead is still without incense?
sentences.i: Or why is Latona worshipped at the altars while my own godhead still goes without incense?
sentences.n: The two clauses are simply set beside each other with no conjunction (asyndeton), and the "while" is left for the reader to supply. `numen ... meum` — she has claimed divinity for herself in two words, and the rest of the speech is the argument for the claim.

sentences.t:
mihi Tantalus auctor,
cui licuit soli superorum tangere mensas,
Pleiadum soror est genetrix mea, maximus Atlas
est avus, aetherium qui fert cervicibus axem;
sentences.l: Tantalus is my founder, to whom alone it was permitted to touch the tables of the gods above; a sister of the Pleiades is my mother; greatest Atlas is my grandfather, who carries the sky's axle on his neck;
sentences.i: My father is Tantalus, the one man ever allowed to touch the gods' own tables; my mother is a sister of the Pleiades; my grandfather is Atlas, the greatest of them, who carries the axle of heaven on his neck;
sentences.n: `mihi Tantalus auctor` is a dative of possession with the verb left out — "to me Tantalus [is] originator"; `auctor` is stronger than "father", meaning the founder of the line. `cui licuit soli` — the impersonal `licet` with a dative, "it was allowed to him": Niobe names Tantalus's privilege at the gods' table and says nothing of what he did there, which is exactly what Latona will bring up at line 213. `cervicibus` is a plural for one neck, ordinary in verse.

sentences.t: Iuppiter alter avus socero quoque glorior illo.
sentences.l: Jupiter is my other grandfather; in him as a father-in-law also I glory.
sentences.i: Jupiter is my other grandfather — and I can boast of him as my father-in-law as well.
sentences.n: `glorior` is a deponent taking the ablative, hence `socero ... illo`, "I glory in him as a father-in-law". The line counts one god twice: Jupiter is her grandfather through Tantalus and her father-in-law through Amphion, and she will not let a single connection go unclaimed. `quoque` here is the plain adverb "also" — but see line 185, where the identical-looking word is not.

sentences.t:
Me gentes metuunt Phrygiae, me regia Cadmi
sub domina est, fidibusque mei commissa mariti
moenia cum populis a meque viroque reguntur.
sentences.l: The Phrygian peoples fear me; the palace of Cadmus is under me as its mistress; and the walls joined together by my husband's lyre-strings are ruled, with their peoples, by me and by my man.
sentences.i: The peoples of Phrygia fear me; the palace of Cadmus has me for its mistress; and the walls his lyre put together, and the peoples inside them, are governed by me and by my husband.
sentences.n: `sub domina est` — "is under [me as] mistress", with `me` in apposition to the object of `sub`. `fidibus ... commissa` is the whole Theban foundation legend in two words: Amphion's playing drew the stones into place, so the walls are literally "put together by strings". Note `a meque viroque`, "both by me and by my husband" — the doubled `-que ... -que` is a verse mannerism, and she puts herself first inside it.

sentences.t:
In quamcumque domus adverti lumina partem,
inmensae spectantur opes. Accedit eodem
digna dea facies.
sentences.l: Into whatever part of the house I have turned my eyes, measureless wealth is seen. There is added to the same place a face worthy of a goddess.
sentences.i: Whatever corner of the house I turn my eyes to, I see measureless wealth. And to the same account add a face fit for a goddess.
sentences.n: `quamcumque ... adverti` — a `-cumque` word with the perfect indicative is Latin's ordinary way of saying "whenever", a general condition, not one past act. `digna` governs the ablative `dea`, "worthy of a goddess". `accedit eodem`, "is added to the same place", keeps a ledger metaphor running through the whole speech: she is totting up assets, and her own face goes into the column.

sentences.t:
Huc natas adice septem
et totidem iuvenes et mox generosque nurusque.
sentences.l: To this add seven daughters and as many young men, and soon sons-in-law and daughters-in-law too.
sentences.n: `adice` (`adjice`) is the imperative of `adicio`, still the accountancy of the speech. `iuvenes`, "young men", are her sons; `totidem` is "just as many". This is where the count of fourteen is said out loud, by her, and the rest of the tale will take it back one at a time.

sentences.t: Quaerite nunc, habeat quam nostra superbia causam,
sentences.l: Ask now what ground my pride has,
sentences.n: `habeat` is subjunctive because `quam ... causam` is an indirect question depending on the imperative `quaerite`. She has said `mihi`, `meum`, `mea` all through the speech and switches here to `nostra`, the royal plural — exactly at the word `superbia`. And `superbia`, "pride", is her own word for her own state of mind, offered without the least embarrassment.

sentences.t:
nescio quoque audete satam Titanida Coeo
Latonam praeferre mihi, cui maxima quondam
exiguam sedem pariturae terra negavit.
sentences.l: and dare to prefer to me Latona, the Titaness born of some Coeus I know not who — to whom, when she was about to give birth, the vast earth once refused a scrap of ground.
sentences.i: and go on, dare to prefer Latona to me — a Titaness fathered by some Coeus or other, a woman the great wide earth once refused the smallest patch of ground when her time came.
sentences.n: Here is the `quoque` trap, and this is the line to learn it on: this is not the adverb "also" but `quo` + `-que`, the connective wedged into the fixed phrase `nescio quis`, "some ... or other". `nescio quo Coeo` is contempt, not ignorance — she is pretending she cannot be bothered to know a Titan's name. `satam ... Coeo` is the same ablative of origin used respectfully of Manto at 157, now used to sneer. `pariturae` is a future participle in the dative agreeing with `cui`, "to her as she was about to give birth".

sentences.t:
Nec caelo nec humo nec aquis dea vestra recepta est:
exsul erat mundi, donec miserata vagantem
“hospita tu terris erras, ego” dixit “in undis”
instabilemque locum Delos dedit.
sentences.l: Neither by heaven nor by earth nor by the waters was your goddess received: she was an exile from the world, until Delos, pitying her as she wandered, said, "You wander a stranger over the lands, I over the waves," and gave her an unsteady place.
sentences.i: Neither sky nor land nor water would take your goddess in: she was an exile from the world, until Delos took pity on her wandering and said, "You drift a stranger over the land, and I over the sea" — and gave her a resting-place that would not hold still.
sentences.n: `dea vestra`, "your goddess" — Niobe will not put Latona's name next to the word for worship; the possessive shoves the goddess onto the crowd and away from herself. `hospita` is feminine and predicative on `tu`, "you as a stranger". Delos's joke works because the island was still floating: neither of them had a fixed place, so the gift is a shared homelessness, and `instabilem locum` is Ovid's flat verdict on it.

sentences.t:
Illa duorum
facta parens: uteri pars haec est septima nostri.
sentences.l: She was made the mother of two: this is a seventh part of my womb.
sentences.i: She became a mother of two — one seventh of what my womb produced.
sentences.n: `facta [est] parens` with the auxiliary dropped, ordinary in verse. `uteri ... nostri pars ... septima` is arithmetic used as an insult: two is a seventh of fourteen, and Niobe reduces another woman's children to a fraction of her own body's output. The royal plural `nostri` again, at the word `womb`.

sentences.t:
Sum felix: quis enim neget hoc? felixque manebo:
hoc quoque quis dubitet?
sentences.l: I am fortunate — for who would deny it? And I shall remain fortunate: who would doubt this too?
sentences.n: Both `neget` and `dubitet` are potential subjunctives — "who *would* deny it?", not "who denies it?" — the same construction as `videres` at 296. She is not asking a question, she is issuing a dare. `felix` is the narrator's word from lines 155–156, where Niobe would have been called the happiest of mothers if she had not thought so herself — and here she thinks so out loud. `quoque` this time really is the adverb.

sentences.t:
tutam me copia fecit,
Maior sum, quam cui possit Fortuna nocere,
multaque ut eripiat, multo mihi plura relinquet.
sentences.l: abundance has made me safe. I am greater than one whom Fortune could harm, and granted that she snatch away much, she will leave me far more.
sentences.i: It is sheer plenty that has made me safe. I stand higher than anything Fortune could damage; let her take much away, she will still leave me far more.
sentences.n: `maior sum quam cui possit Fortuna nocere` is a compressed idiom: comparative + `quam` + a relative clause of characteristic, "greater than [the sort of person] to whom Fortune could do harm"; `nocere` takes the dative, which is why it is `cui` and not `quem`. `ut eripiat` is concessive, "granted that she takes", and `multo plura` uses the ablative of degree of difference, "more by much". This is a line a reader may have met quoted on its own, and everything after it in the tale exists to answer it.

sentences.t:
Excessere metum mea iam bona. Fingite demi
huic aliquid populo natorum posse meorum,
non tamen ad numerum redigar spoliata duorum,
sentences.l: My blessings have by now gone past fear. Imagine that something can be taken away from this whole population of my children: even so, robbed, I shall not be brought down to the number of two,
sentences.i: My fortunes have outgrown fear by now. Suppose something could be taken from this whole nation of children of mine — even stripped, I would not be cut down to a total of two,
sentences.n: `Excessere` = `excesserunt`, the `-ēre` perfect for the second time (you met `placuere` at 154). `metum` is its direct object: her goods have not merely escaped fear, they have overtaken it. `populo natorum`, "a population of children", is the census language of the whole speech pushed one step further. `fingite ... demi ... posse` is an imperative with an indirect statement under it, and the infinitive `demi` is passive: "imagine it to be possible for something to be taken away".

sentences.t: Latonae turbam: qua quantum distat ab orba?
sentences.l: Latona's crowd: with that, how far is she from being childless?
sentences.i: Latona's great multitude. With that for a crowd, how far off childless is she?
sentences.n: `turbam` is in apposition to "the number of two" in the line before, and it is pure sarcasm: `turba` is the word for a mob or a press of people, used here of two. `qua` is its ablative, "with that crowd"; `quantum` is an adverbial accusative of extent, "how far". Mark the word `orba`, "bereft of children": Niobe throws it at Latona here, Latona reports it back at 212, and the narrator will use it of Niobe herself at 301.

sentences.t:
Ite, satis, propere ite, sacri est laurumque capillis
ponite.”
sentences.l: Go — enough — go quickly; there is enough of the rite; and put the laurel off your hair."
sentences.i: Go on, that is enough of it; go quickly. The rite has had its due. Take the laurel out of your hair."
sentences.n: `satis ... sacri est` — `satis` with a partitive genitive, "enough of the rite"; `sacrum` in the singular is the rite itself. `ponite` here is "lay aside, put off", the sense of `deponere`, which the very next line uses of the same action. Some editions print `satis pro re sacri est`, "there has been enough of the rite for the occasion", where Magnus prints `propere ite`, and the sentence reads more smoothly that way; Magnus is the text here.

sentences.t:
Deponunt et sacra infecta relinquunt,
quodque licet tacito venerantur murmure numen.
sentences.l: They lay it aside and leave the rite unperformed, and — so far as is allowed — they worship the divinity with a silent murmur.
sentences.i: They lay it aside and leave the rite unfinished, and do the one thing still permitted them: worship the goddess under their breath.
sentences.n: `quodque licet` is a parenthetical relative, "and the thing which is allowed" — all that is left to them once a queen has given an order. `infecta` is `in-` + `facta`, "not done", nothing to do with infection; it is the standard word for a rite left incomplete, which is itself an offence. `tacito ... murmure` is a two-word paradox: a murmur that makes no sound.

sentences.t:
Indignata dea est summoque in vertice Cynthi
talibus est dictis gemina cum prole locuta:
sentences.l: The goddess was outraged, and on the topmost peak of Cynthus she spoke to her twin offspring with words like these:
sentences.n: Cynthus is the mountain of Delos — the island of line 191, the one scrap of ground that took Latona in, and Ovid puts her back on it to answer the sneer about it. `gemina ... prole` is a collective singular for the two of them together, Apollo and Diana. `talibus ... dictis` is an ablative of means and the standard epic formula for opening a speech, so a reader learns to hear it as "and this is what she said".

sentences.t:
“En ego vestra parens, vobis animosa creatis,
et nisi Iunoni nulli cessura dearum,
sentences.l: "See, I, your mother, proud in your having been born, and ready to yield to no goddess but Juno,
sentences.i: "Look at me: your mother, proud because you were born to me, and ready to give way to no goddess except Juno —
sentences.n: `vobis ... creatis` is an ablative absolute doing the work of a causal clause: a noun and a participle in the ablative, self-contained, which English almost always has to open out into "because...". You will meet nine more of these before the tale is over, and one of them will carry Amphion's suicide. `cessura` is a future participle used as a plain adjective, "one who would yield"; `cedo` takes the dative, hence `Iunoni` and `nulli`.

sentences.t:
an dea sim dubitor perque omnia saecula cultis
arceor, o nati, nisi vos succurritis, aris.
sentences.l: I am doubted whether I am a goddess, and I am shut out, my children, from altars worshipped through all the ages, unless you come to my aid.
sentences.i: It is being questioned whether I am a goddess at all, and unless you two come to my help, my children, I am barred from altars that have had worship through every age.
sentences.n: `dubitor` is a personal passive where English needs an impersonal: "I am doubted [as to] whether I am a goddess", with the indirect question `an dea sim` hanging on it. `arceor ... aris` is an ablative of separation with no preposition, "kept away from the altars". The word order buries `aris` at the very end, after the conditional clause, so the altars are the last thing her sons hear — which is what she wants them thinking about.

sentences.t:
Nec dolor hic solus: diro convicia facto
Tantalis adiecit vosque est postponere natis
ausa suis,
sentences.l: Nor is this the only grief: the daughter of Tantalus has added insults to the dreadful deed, and has dared to put you behind her own children,
sentences.i: And that is not the whole of the injury: Tantalus's daughter has piled abuse on top of the outrage itself, and has dared to rank you below her own children,
sentences.n: `Tantalis` is a Greek patronymic, "the daughter of Tantalus" — Latona will not say Niobe's name any more than Niobe would say hers. `diro ... facto` is dative with `adiecit`, "added to the deed": the deed is the stopping of the rite, the `convicia` are the speech that went with it. `postponere` puts its accusative below its dative — `vos ... natis suis`, "you below her own children" — so the dative names the one ranked higher, and the charge is that Niobe put Apollo and Diana beneath her own children. It is the exact mirror of Niobe's own `praeponere` at 170 and `praeferre` at 186, where the dative was the one ranked lower: her construction turned back on her.

sentences.t:
et me, quod in ipsam reccidat, orbam,
dixit et exhibuit linguam scelerata paternam.”
sentences.l: and she called me childless — may that fall back on the woman herself — and, wicked creature, showed her father's tongue."
sentences.i: and she called me childless — may the word come back on her own head — and in her wickedness showed that she has her father's tongue."
sentences.n: `quod in ipsam reccidat` is a parenthetical curse with the subjunctive of wish, "which may it fall back upon her"; the rest of the tale is that wish being granted. `orbam` is the word Niobe used of Latona at 200. `linguam ... paternam` is the charge under the charge: Tantalus's crime was what came out of his mouth, and Latona says the daughter has inherited it. `scelerata` is an adjective used as a noun, "the wicked one", and it is Latona's word for Niobe, not the poem's.

sentences.t:
Adiectura preces erat his Latona relatis:
“desine!” Phoebus ait: “poenae mora longa querella est.”
sentences.l: These things having been recounted, Latona was about to add prayers, when "Stop!" said Phoebus; "a long complaint is a delay of the punishment."
sentences.i: Having recounted all this, Latona was on the point of adding a plea, when Phoebus said: "Stop. A long complaint is only the punishment put off."
sentences.n: `adiectura erat` is the active periphrastic — future participle plus `esse`, "was on the point of adding" — and the son cuts her off before she can get the request out; she never actually asks for anything. `his relatis` is another ablative absolute, "these things having been recounted". Phoebus's line has the shape of a proverb: `mora` and `querella` are both nominative, so the sentence can be turned either way round and mean the same thing.

sentences.t:
Dixit idem Phoebe: celerique per aera lapsu
contigerant tecti Calmeida nubibus arcem.
sentences.l: Phoebe said the same; and with a swift glide through the air, covered by clouds, they had reached the [Cadmean?] citadel.
sentences.i: Phoebe said the same — and with one swift glide through the air, hidden in cloud, they were already on the [Cadmean] citadel.
sentences.n: `tecti nubibus` is nominative plural and agrees with the twins, not with the citadel: it is they who are wrapped in cloud, the ordinary epic way of moving a god unseen. The pluperfect `contigerant` is the speed of the thing — by the time the sentence ends they have already arrived. **`Calmeida` is not a Latin word: the digitized text of the edition is damaged at this point.** The word is certainly `Cadmeida`, a Greek feminine accusative meaning "Cadmean", i.e. the citadel of Thebes, the city Cadmus founded. It is printed here exactly as the edition has it, unemended.

sentences.t:
Planus erat lateque patens prope moenia campus,
adsiduis pulsatus equis, ubi turba rotarum
duraque mollierat subiectas ungula glaebas.
sentences.l: There was a level plain, opening wide near the walls, beaten by constant horses, where the throng of wheels and the hard hoof had softened the clods beneath.
sentences.i: Near the walls lay a flat, wide-open field, pounded by horses day after day, where crowding wheels and hard hooves had worked the clods underfoot soft.
sentences.n: "There was a place..." is epic's standard way of setting a scene, and in Ovid it is nearly always a warning that something is about to happen in it. `adsiduis pulsatus equis` is an ablative of means with a perfect participle; Magnus's `adsiduis` for `assiduis` is the edition's spelling and is kept. `mollierat` is transitive — the traffic had *made soft*, churned up, the ground — and the detail matters because in nine lines a boy will come off a horse onto it.

sentences.t:
Pars ibi de septem genitis Amphione fortes
conscendunt in equos Tyrioque rubentia suco
terga premunt auroque graves moderantur habenas.
sentences.l: There a part of the seven begotten of Amphion mount onto strong horses and press backs reddened with Tyrian dye and handle reins heavy with gold.
sentences.i: There some of the seven sons of Amphion swing up onto strong horses, settle onto saddle-cloths red with Tyrian purple, and take up reins weighted with gold.
sentences.n: `genitis Amphione` is the ablative of origin again, "begotten from Amphion". `terga` is literally "backs" and means the horses' backs with their coverings; `Tyrio ... suco` is the purple dye of Tyre, the most expensive colour in the ancient world, so the boys ride out wearing the family's balance sheet. `pars ... conscendunt` has a singular collective subject with a plural verb — Latin permits the agreement by sense, English mostly does not.

sentences.t:
E quibus Ismenus, qui matri sarcina quondam
prima suae fuerat, dum certum flectit in orbem
quadrupedis cursus spumantiaque ora coercet,
“ei mihi!” conclamat
sentences.l: Of these Ismenus, who had once been his mother's first burden, while he bends his horse's course into a set circle and reins in its foaming mouth, cries out, "Ah, me!"
sentences.i: One of them, Ismenus — who had once been the first weight his mother carried — is turning his horse's course into a tight circle and holding in its foaming mouth when he cries out, "Ah, me!"
sentences.n: `sarcina ... prima` is the ordinary word for a pack or a load, used of a child in the womb — a tender phrase, and placed here so that the first son to die is the first she carried. `quadrupedis` is a noun, "the four-footed one", a poetic way of not saying "horse". `dum` with the present indicative inside past narrative is normal and means "while", not "as long as". `ora` is a poetic plural for the horse's one mouth. And `E quibus` opens the sentence with a relative doing a conjunction's work — "and of these" — a habit Latin has and English has not; it comes again at 252, 279, 287, 290 and 298, and each time the right English is "and".

sentences.t:
medioque in pectore fixa
tela gerit, frenisque manu moriente remissis
in latus a dextro paulatim defluit armo.
sentences.l: and in the middle of his chest he carries a shaft fixed there, and with the reins let go by his dying hand he slides down little by little onto his side, from the right shoulder.
sentences.i: and there is a shaft fixed in the middle of his chest; his dying hand lets the reins go and he slides slowly down sideways, off the horse's right shoulder.
sentences.n: `frenis ... remissis` is another ablative absolute, and `manu moriente` sits inside it: the hand is dying before the man is. `defluit` is the verb for water running downhill, and `paulatim`, "little by little", holds the whole fall in slow motion — the first death in the tale is given the longest exit. `armo` is the shoulder of an animal, not a man's, so it is the horse's right shoulder he comes off over.

sentences.t:
Proximus, audito sonitu per inane pharetrae,
frena dabat Sipylus,
sentences.l: Next, with the sound of the quiver heard through the empty air, Sipylus was giving his horse the reins,
sentences.i: Next, Sipylus, hearing the quiver's rattle come through the empty air, was giving his horse its head,
sentences.n: `audito sonitu ... pharetrae` is an ablative absolute again, and it carries one of Ovid's best details: nobody sees the archer, they hear the arrows knock together in his quiver. `per inane` — `inane` is a noun, "the empty", the void. `frena dabat`, "was giving the reins", means letting them out, letting the horse run — the exact opposite of the `coercet` of the brother in the last unit. The name is his mother's mountain from line 149.

sentences.t:
veluti cum praescius imbris
nube fugit visa pendentiaque undique rector
carbasa deducit, ne qua levis effluat aura.
sentences.l: just as when a helmsman foreknowing rain flees at the sight of a cloud and hauls down the canvas hanging on every side, so that no light breath may slip away.
sentences.i: the way a helmsman who can read the coming rain runs the moment he sees a cloud, and lets down the canvas hanging all around him so that not a breath of wind goes to waste.
sentences.n: `nube ... visa` is the third ablative absolute in five lines — `frenis remissis` at 228, `audito sonitu` at 230, and now this; once you can see the shape — noun + participle, both ablative, no preposition — the construction stops being an obstacle. `carbasa` is a Greek loan-word for fine linen sailcloth. `ne qua ... aura` uses `qua` for `aliqua`, "any" (the indefinite drops its `ali-` after `ne`, `si` and `num`). The simile is about wringing out the last of the available speed, which is what Sipylus is doing when the arrow arrives.

sentences.t:
Frena tamen dantem non evitabile telum
consequitur; summaque tremens cervice sagitta
haesit, et exstabat nudum de gutture ferrum.
sentences.l: Still, as he gives the reins a shaft not to be dodged overtakes him; and quivering, the arrow stuck at the top of his neck, and the bare iron was standing out from his throat.
sentences.i: But even as he gives it the reins the shaft catches him, and there is no dodging it. The arrow stuck quivering at the top of his neck, and the bare iron stood out through his throat.
sentences.n: `dantem` is a participle used as a noun, "the one giving [the reins]", and it repeats `frena dabat` from two lines back so that the arrow lands in the middle of the same action. `non evitabile` splits the negative off the adjective — "not-to-be-avoided". Watch the tenses: `consequitur` is present and `haesit` and `exstabat` are past, so the arrow arrives *now* and is already fixed. `summa ... cervice` is the top of the neck, and the point comes through at the front.

sentences.t:
Ille, ut erat, pronus per crura admissa iubasque
volvitur et calido tellurem sanguine foedat.
sentences.l: He, just as he was, pitched forward, rolls down over the galloping legs and the mane, and fouls the earth with hot blood.
sentences.i: He goes over just as he was, thrown forward across the racing legs and the mane, and fouls the ground with hot blood.
sentences.n: `ut erat`, "just as he was", keeps the body in the posture the living man had put it in — Ovid does this deliberately and will do it again at 244. `crura admissa`: `admittere` is the technical term for letting a horse out at full gallop, so "the let-out legs" are legs at a run, and the horse has not stopped. `foedat` is stronger than "stains": it is "defiles, makes foul", the word for spoiling something clean.

sentences.l: Unlucky Phaedimus, and Tantalus, heir of his grandfather's name, when they had put an end to their usual exercise, had passed on to the youthful work of the gleaming wrestling-floor;
sentences.i: Poor Phaedimus, and Tantalus who carried his grandfather's name, had finished their usual exercise and moved on to the young men's work of the oiled wrestling-floor;
sentences.n: `imposuere` = `imposuerunt`, the `-ēre` perfect for the third time in this part. `aviti nominis heres` — the boy is named for the Tantalus of line 172, Niobe's father; the name is called an inheritance, and it is a reminder of whose blood is being punished. `nitidae ... palaestrae`, "gleaming", because wrestlers oiled their bodies; `iuvenale opus` is the exercise proper to their age, which is the age they will not get past.

sentences.t:
et iam contulerant arto luctantia nexu
pectora pectoribus, cum tento concita nervo,
sicut erant iuncti, traiecit utrumque sagitta.
sentences.l: and already they had brought chests together against chests, wrestling in a tight grip, when an arrow, driven from a taut string, went through them both, just as they were, locked together.
sentences.i: and they had already brought chest to chest, straining in a close hold, when an arrow loosed from a drawn string went through the pair of them, just as they were, locked together.
sentences.n: `pectora pectoribus` is the same noun twice in two cases, accusative beside dative — how Latin says "chest to chest" with no preposition at all, and the doubling *is* the wrestling hold. `tento ... nervo` is an ablative of means with `concita` — the arrow "set moving by a taut string"; `nervus` is the bowstring, the same word that will sound on its own at 286. `sicut erant iuncti` repeats the trick of `ut erat` at 237: the body left in the shape the living man made, which is why one arrow can do for two.

sentences.t:
Ingemuere simul, simul incurvata dolore
membra solo posuere, simul suprema iacentes
lumina versarunt, animam simul exhalarunt.
sentences.l: They groaned together; together they laid on the ground limbs bent double with pain; together, lying there, they turned their eyes for the last time; together they breathed out their life.
sentences.n: Four clauses, four `simul`s, and the word moves to a different position each time — the sentence is *about* two people doing everything at the same instant, and the repetition is the twinning. `Ingemuere` and `posuere` are the `-ēre` perfect again; `versarunt` and `exhalarunt` are contracted from `versaverunt` and `exhalaverunt`, another poetic shortening worth recognizing on sight. `suprema ... lumina`, "eyes for the last time", is an adjective doing an adverb's work.

sentences.t:
Adspicit Alphenor laniataque pectora plangens
advolat, ut gelidos complexibus adlevet artus,
inque pio cadit officio:
sentences.l: Alphenor sees it and, beating his torn breast, flies to them, to lift the cold limbs in his arms — and in that dutiful office he falls:
sentences.i: Alphenor sees, and beating his own breast till it is torn he runs to them, to raise the cold bodies in his arms — and falls in the middle of that act of duty:
sentences.n: `laniata ... pectora plangens` is ancient mourning done at a run: `plangere` is to beat the breast, and `laniata` means he has already torn it doing so. `pium officium` is the technical phrase for what is owed to the dead — obligation rather than sentiment, the same `pius` as the prayers at line 161 — and Ovid kills him inside it. `ut ... adlevet` is a purpose clause.

sentences.t:
nam Delius illi
intima fatifero rupit praecordia ferro.
sentences.l: for the Delian burst his innermost vitals with death-bringing iron.
sentences.i: for the god of Delos burst the inmost parts of his chest with death-bearing iron.
sentences.n: `Delius`, "the Delian", is Apollo named from Delos — the island Niobe called an unsteady scrap of ground at line 191. Ovid chooses the epithet rather than the name, and the sneer is what gives it its edge. `illi` is a dative of the person affected where English wants a possessive: "burst the vitals *for him*" = "his vitals". `praecordia` are the organs behind the breastbone — diaphragm, heart and lungs together.

sentences.t:
Quod simul eductum est, pars est pulmonis in hamis
eruta cumque anima cruor est effusus in auras.
sentences.l: And as soon as it was drawn out, part of his lung was torn away on the barbs, and along with his breath his blood was poured out into the air.
sentences.i: And the moment the iron was pulled out, part of his lung came away on the barbs, and his blood went out into the air along with his breath.
sentences.n: `Quod` opens the sentence as a connecting relative — "and this", picking up `ferro` from the line before. Latin begins sentences this way constantly and English almost always wants "and it" or "and that". `in hamis` are the barbs of the arrowhead, which is exactly why drawing an arrow out does more damage than leaving it in. `cum anima` puts the breath and the blood into one phrase and lets them leave together.

sentences.t:
At non intonsum simplex Damasichthona vulnus
adficit. Ictus erat qua crus esse incipit et qua
mollia nervosus facit internodia poples.
sentences.l: But a single wound does not afflict unshorn Damasichthon. He had been struck where the shin begins, and where the sinewy back of the knee makes the joints pliant.
sentences.i: But one wound is not enough for long-haired Damasichthon. He was hit where the shin starts, at the point where the sinewy back of the knee keeps the joints supple.
sentences.n: `Damasichthona` keeps its Greek accusative ending in `-a` instead of the Latin `-em`; Ovid preserves Greek forms for Greek names, and you will see `Nioben` doing the same at 287. `intonsum`, "unshorn", marks him as still a boy: young men cut their hair at coming of age. `poples` is the hollow at the back of the knee and `internodia` the stretch of limb between two joints, so Ovid is naming a boundary rather than a body part: the arrow goes in exactly where the lower leg starts. `mollia ... internodia` is object plus predicate adjective — the hough "makes the joints pliant" — and it is that pliancy that lets the iron in. `simplex ... vulnus` sets up the variation: this brother gets two.

sentences.t:
Dumque manu temptat trahere exitiabile telum,
altera per iugulum pennis tenus acta sagitta est.
sentences.l: And while he is trying with his hand to pull out the deadly shaft, a second arrow was driven through his throat as far as the feathers.
sentences.n: `pennis tenus` — `tenus` is a postposition, standing after its noun and taking the ablative: "up to the feathers", i.e. buried to the fletching. `dum` with the present again inside past narrative. Note the shape of the death: it is his own hands being busy with the first arrow that leaves him open to the second, which is Ovid varying the manner rather than repeating it.

sentences.t:
Expulit hanc sanguis, seque eiaculatus in altum
emicat et longe terebrata prosilit aura.
sentences.l: The blood drove this one out, and hurling itself on high it darts out and springs far off through the bored air.
sentences.i: The blood forced that arrow back out, and jetting upward it shoots clear and springs far off, drilling the air as it goes.
sentences.n: `se ... eiaculatus` is a deponent participle with a reflexive object, "having hurled itself": the blood is the subject of three verbs in a row and behaves like something alive. `terebrata ... aura` is ablative — the jet is imagined boring a channel through the air, `terebra` being the carpenter's auger. `emicat`, `prosilit` and the participle all mean roughly "shoot out", stacked up so that one image runs on longer than it needs to.

sentences.t:
Ultimus Ilioneus non profectura precando
bracchia sustulerat, “di” que “o communiter omnes,”
dixerat ignarus non omnes esse rogandos
“parcite.”
sentences.l: Last, Ilioneus had raised arms that would gain nothing by praying, and had said, "Gods — oh, all of you together — spare!", not knowing that not all of them had to be asked.
sentences.i: Ilioneus, last of them, had lifted up arms that praying would do no good with, and had said, "Gods, oh, all of you together — spare me!" — not knowing that not all of them needed the asking.
sentences.n: `non profectura` is a future participle used as the narrator's bitter aside — "arms that were not going to succeed" — so Ovid tells you the prayer fails before the boy has made it. `non omnes esse rogandos` is an indirect statement with the gerundive of obligation: only two gods had to be begged, and the child scatters his prayer across the whole pantheon. `parcite` is absolute — one word, no object at all; the boy does not get as far as saying what he wants spared, and the literal leaves the gap where Latin leaves it while the idiomatic supplies the "me" English expects. Turning aside to comment on a character's ignorance is among the poem's most constant habits, and you will meet it on every page.

sentences.t:
Motus erat, cum iam revocabile telum
non fuit, arquitenens. Minimo tamen occidit ille
vulnere, non alte percusso corde sagitta.
sentences.l: The bow-holder had been moved — at a point when the shaft could no longer be called back. Still, he died of the smallest wound, his heart not struck deep by the arrow.
sentences.i: The archer had been moved — by which time the shaft could not be called back. He died of the smallest wound of them all, the arrow not driven deep into his heart.
sentences.n: `arquitenens`, "bow-holder", is a solemn old cult-title of Apollo, and Ovid saves it for the one moment the god relents — too late. `revocabile` is an adjective in `-bilis` doing the work of a whole clause, "able to be called back". `percusso corde` is another ablative absolute, and it carries the pathos of the whole sequence: the seventh son dies of the least of the seven wounds, and the arrow barely went in.

sentences.t:
Fama mali populique dolor lacrimaeque suorum
tam subitae matrem certam fecere ruinae,
mirantem potuisse, irascentemque, quod ausi
hoc essent superi, quod tantum iuris haberent.
sentences.l: The report of the disaster and the grief of the people and the tears of her own made the mother certain of a ruin so sudden — wondering that it could be done, and angry that the gods above had dared this, that they had so much right.
sentences.i: Word of the disaster, the grief of the city, the tears of her own household made the mother certain of a ruin so sudden — amazed that such a thing was possible, and furious that the gods above had dared it and had so much right on their side.
sentences.n: `certam ... ruinae` — an adjective of knowing taking a genitive, "sure of the ruin". `mirantem potuisse` is compressed even for Ovid: an indirect statement with no subject expressed at all, "that [it] had been able [to happen]". `quod ... essent` and `quod ... haberent` take the subjunctive because the reason given is hers, not the narrator's: she is angry *on the grounds that*, as she sees it, they dared. `tantum iuris` is a partitive genitive, "so much of right" — she is still arguing about jurisdiction with seven sons dead.

sentences.t:
Nam pater Amphion ferro per pectus adacto
finierat moriens pariter cum luce dolorem.
sentences.l: For the father, Amphion, with iron driven through his breast, had in dying ended his grief and the light together.
sentences.i: For their father Amphion had driven iron through his chest, and dying had put an end to his grief and to the daylight at one stroke.
sentences.n: `ferro ... adacto` is an ablative absolute doing the work of a main clause — the suicide is told entirely inside a subordinate phrase, and English has to open it out to say it at all. `pariter cum luce`, "equally with the light": `lux` for "life" is standard, and the two endings are simultaneous. This is the husband whose lyre built the walls at 178; the poem gives him a line and a half and goes back to Niobe.

sentences.t:
Heu quantum haec Niobe Niobe distabat ab illa,
quae modo Latois populum submoverat aris
et mediam tulerat gressus resupina per urbem,
invidiosa suis, at nunc miseranda vel hosti.
sentences.l: Alas, how far this Niobe stood from that Niobe, who a moment ago had driven the people back from Latona's altars and had carried her steps through the middle of the city with her head thrown back — envied by her own, and now to be pitied even by an enemy.
sentences.i: How far this Niobe stood from that one — who only a moment before had pushed the people back from Latona's altars and walked through the middle of the city with her head high, the envy of her own people, and now to be pitied even by an enemy.
sentences.n: `haec Niobe Niobe ... ab illa` — the name printed twice, side by side in the middle of the line, with `haec` and `illa` pulling the two Niobes apart from either end. The figure *is* the sentence, and it is why the line gets quoted on its own. `Latois ... aris` is a possessive adjective, "Latona's". `resupina` means bent backwards, head up: a posture word, and standing next to `invidiosa suis` it turns into a judgement.

sentences.t:
Corporibus gelidis incumbit et ordine nullo
oscula dispensat natos suprema per omnes.
sentences.l: She falls upon the cold bodies and in no order deals out her last kisses among all her sons.
sentences.i: She throws herself down on the cold bodies and gives out her last kisses among all her sons, in no order at all.
sentences.n: `incumbit` takes the dative, hence `corporibus`. `ordine nullo`, "in no order", is the detail that does the work: the woman whose whole speech was a count and a ranking has stopped counting. And `dispensat` is a word from managing a household's stores, "portions out" — even her grief comes out in the ledger-language of the boast.

sentences.t:
A quibus ad caelum liventia bracchia tollens
“pascere, crudelis, nostro, Latona, dolore,
pascere” ait “satiaque meo tua pectora luctu:
sentences.l: Lifting from them to heaven arms bruised black, "Feed, cruel Latona, on my grief," she says, "feed, and glut your heart with my mourning:
sentences.i: Lifting arms bruised black from them towards heaven: "Feed on my grief, Latona, you cruel thing," she says, "feed — and stuff your heart full with my mourning:
sentences.n: `pascere` is not the infinitive but the passive imperative of `pasco`, used in the middle sense — "feed yourself", the way a beast is put to pasture. Ovid places it twice, at the start of one line and the start of the next, so the demand is made and then repeated across the line-break. `liventia bracchia` are arms gone livid — bruised from her own beating of them in mourning. `A quibus` is a connecting relative, "and from these".

sentences.t:
“Corque ferum satia” dixit, “per funera septem”
efferor.
sentences.l: "and glut your savage heart," she said; "through seven deaths I am carried out to burial.
sentences.i: "Glut that savage heart of yours," she said. "Through seven funerals I am carried to the grave.
sentences.n: `efferor` is the technical verb for carrying a body out of the house for burial — the root of `funus efferre` — and she uses it of herself, alive: she is the one being buried, seven times over. `funera` means both the deaths and the processions, and Latin does not make you choose. The quotation marks here are the edition's own and are printed exactly as Magnus has them; the speech evidently runs straight on through `efferor`.

sentences.t:
Exsulta victrixque inimica triumpha.
Cur autem victrix? miserae mihi plura supersunt,
quam tibi felici: post tot quoque funera vinco.”
sentences.l: Exult, and triumph, my victorious enemy. But why victorious? More are left to me in my wretchedness than to you in your good fortune: even after so many deaths, I win."
sentences.i: Exult; hold your triumph, my enemy, my conqueror. But why conqueror? Wretched as I am, I still have more left than you have in all your good fortune: even after so many funerals, I win."
sentences.n: `triumpha` is the verb of the Roman triumph, the victory procession through the city — Niobe hands her enemy a Roman ceremony to hold. `victrix` and `inimica` are vocatives — Niobe is speaking straight at Latona. Outside the second declension the vocative is simply identical to the nominative, so nothing in the form itself tells you it is an address: only the imperatives `exsulta` and `triumpha` beside it do. `miserae mihi ... quam tibi felici` sets `misera` against `felix`, the word she claimed for herself at 193: she has lost the word and is still doing the arithmetic with it. `quoque` here is the adverb, "even".

sentences.t:
Dixerat, et sonuit contento nervus ab arcu.
Qui praeter Nioben unam conterruit omnes:
illa malo est audax.
sentences.l: She had finished, and a string sounded from a drawn bow. It terrified everyone except Niobe alone: she is made bold by disaster.
sentences.i: She had finished, and a bowstring sang from a drawn bow. The sound terrified them all except Niobe: her own ruin is what makes her reckless.
sentences.n: `Qui` is a connecting relative picking up `nervus` — "and this [sound]": it is the noise, not the string, that does the terrifying. `Nioben` is the Greek accusative again, like `Damasichthona` at 254. `malo est audax` is an ablative of cause: the disaster itself is what makes her bold. And note the tense — after a long run of perfects the verb goes present and the narrative stops dead on her.

sentences.t:
Stabant cum vestibus atris
ante toros fratrum demisso crine sorores.
sentences.l: The sisters were standing in black clothing before their brothers' biers, with their hair let down.
sentences.n: `demisso crine` is one more ablative absolute, this time describing a costume: loosened hair was formal mourning for women, exactly as the black clothing was, so both halves of the line are ritual rather than dishevelment. `toros` are couches — the bodies are laid out on them for the wake, and that is what the sisters are standing at when the second archer starts.

sentences.t:
E quibus una trahens haerentia viscere tela
imposito fratri moribunda relanguit ore:
sentences.l: One of them, drawing out the shafts that stuck in his flesh, with her face laid upon her brother, dying, went slack.
sentences.i: One of them, pulling out the shafts lodged in her brother's flesh, laid her face down on him and went limp in death.
sentences.n: `imposito fratri ... ore` is an ablative absolute with a dative inside it: "her face having been laid on her brother" — the literal keeps it as a phrase rather than making the girl the subject of a second verb, because that is what the Latin does. `haerentia ... tela` is plural: either she draws out more than one shaft or it is the poetic plural you have already met in `ora` at 226 and `cervicibus` at 175, and the literal keeps the plural rather than choosing for you. `relanguit` is a rare compound — "went slack again", the body letting go of its own hold. Look at what she was doing when it happened: she dies drawing an arrow out of a brother, which is very nearly the death Alphenor died at 250, and Ovid is rhyming the two halves of the massacre.

sentences.t:
altera solari miseram conata parentem
conticuit subito duplicataque vulnere tota est.
oraque compressit, nisi postquam spiritus ibat.
sentences.l: Another, having tried to comfort her wretched mother, fell silent all at once and was doubled right over by a wound; and she pressed her lips shut, except after her breath was going.
sentences.i: Another, who had tried to comfort her wretched mother, broke off all at once and was doubled right over by a wound; and she kept her mouth shut, and opened it only when her breath was already going.
sentences.n: `conata` is the deponent participle of `conor` and is concessive here — she tried, and did not finish; `conticuit` is an inceptive compound, "fell silent", and the whole force of it is what she fell silent in the middle of. Some editions print `vulnere caeco`, "by an unseen wound", where Magnus prints `tota`. The last line is one many editors have suspected of being a later addition, since it follows a sentence that is already complete; Magnus prints it, and it is kept here as the edition has it. It is also obscure in itself: `nisi postquam` after `compressit` will not construe smoothly, and the best that can be got out of it is that she held her mouth shut and unclosed it only as the breath was leaving her. That obscurity is part of why the line is suspected — the literal keeps the strain visible and the idiomatic guesses at the sense, and the reader should know the two layers are further apart here than anywhere else in the tale.

sentences.t:
Haec frustra fugiens collabitur, illa sorori
inmoritur, latet haec, illam trepidare videres.
sentences.l: This one, fleeing in vain, collapses; that one dies upon a sister; this one hides; that one you would have seen trembling.
sentences.i: One collapses running, for nothing; one dies on top of a sister; one hides; one you could see shaking.
sentences.n: Four sisters in a line and a half, marked off only by `haec ... illa ... haec ... illam`, "this one ... that one", with not a name among them — and only two of the four are actually said to die: one collapses, one dies on a sister, one is merely hiding and one merely shaking. It is `sex`, "six", in the next line that tells the reader all four are dead. After giving every son a name and a manner, Ovid takes the names away, and the anonymity is the effect. `inmoritur` takes the dative, "dies upon". `videres` is a potential subjunctive addressed to the reader — "you would have seen" — one of the poem's habitual turns aside to put you in the room.

sentences.t:
Sexque datis leto diversaque vulnera passis
ultima restabat.
sentences.l: And with six given over to death and having suffered wounds each unlike the rest, the last one was left.
sentences.i: With six of them handed over to death, each by a different wound, one was left.
sentences.n: One more ablative absolute, and a double one: `datis` and `passis` both govern `sex`, and the second, from the deponent `patior`, is active in meaning — "having suffered". `diversa ... vulnera` is Ovid saying out loud what the last eighty lines have been doing: no two of these deaths are the same, and the variation is the design, not an accident of the telling.

sentences.t:
Quam toto corpore mater,
tota veste tegens “unam minimamque relinque
de multis minimam posco” clamavit “et unam.”
sentences.l: Her the mother, covering her with her whole body, with her whole robe, cried out: "Leave me one, and the smallest! Out of so many I ask for the smallest — and for one."
sentences.i: Over her the mother threw her whole body and her whole robe, and cried: "Leave me one — the smallest! Out of so many I am asking for the smallest, and for one."
sentences.n: `Quam` is a connecting relative, "and her". `toto corpore, tota veste` is the gesture in its grammar: she covers the girl twice, once with herself and once with her clothes. And the speech reverses the boast exactly — at 182 she counted upward, seven and seven and sons-in-law to come; here she asks for the number one and calls it the smallest, and says both words twice. `minimam` means youngest as well as least.

sentences.t:
Dumque rogat, pro qua rogat, occidit. Orba resedit
exanimes inter natos natasque virumque,
deriguitque malis.
sentences.l: And while she asks, the one she asks for dies. Childless, she sat down among her lifeless sons and daughters and husband, and went rigid with her sufferings.
sentences.i: And while she is still asking, the girl she is asking for dies. Childless, she sat down among her lifeless sons and daughters and her husband, and stiffened with her sufferings.
sentences.n: `pro qua rogat` is a relative clause folded into the sentence it belongs to — "the one on whose behalf she asks" — and the point is that `rogat` and `occidit` sit in the same half-line: the asking and the dying occupy the same instant. `Orba` is the word Niobe threw at Latona at 200 and Latona reported back at 212; the poem holds it until now and then puts it first in the sentence. `deriguit` is inceptive, "began to be stiff" — the transformation starts here and everything after it is the detail.

sentences.t:
Nullos movet aura capillos,
in vultu color est sine sanguine, lumina maestis
stant inmota genis, nihil est in imagine vivum.
sentences.l: The breeze moves no hair of hers; in her face there is a colour without blood; her eyes stand unmoving in her mourning cheeks; there is nothing alive in the likeness.
sentences.n: Four clauses laid side by side with no connectives at all (asyndeton), each taking away a different sign of life — hair, colour, eyes, and then the whole at once. `color ... sine sanguine` is a colour with nothing behind it. `imago` is the word for a statue or a painted likeness, so before the stone is ever named the reader has been told she is a work of art, and told that there is nothing living in it.

sentences.t:
Ipsa quoque interius cum duro lingua palato
congelat, et venae desistunt posse moveri;
sentences.l: Her very tongue too freezes hard inside, along with the hard palate, and her veins cease to be able to be moved;
sentences.i: Inside her mouth the tongue itself freezes hard along with the palate, and her veins stop being able to move;
sentences.n: `quoque` here is the plain adverb "also" — worth checking against line 185, where the identical-looking word was `quo` + `-que`. `duro ... palato`: the palate is hard anyway, so the epithet is doing double duty as the ordinary description and as the thing now happening to her. `desistunt posse moveri` piles three constructions up — "cease to be able to be moved", with a passive infinitive under an active one — and the clumsiness is the point: everything has to pass through one more layer before it can stop.

sentences.t:
nec flecti cervix nec bracchia reddere motus
nec pes ire potest; intra quoque viscera saxum est.
sentences.l: and the neck cannot bend, nor the arms give back a movement, nor the foot walk; inside too, her vitals are stone.
sentences.i: her neck cannot bend, her arms cannot answer with a movement, her foot cannot walk; inside as well, her flesh is stone.
sentences.n: One `potest` at the end serves all three `nec` clauses, so a single verb has to carry the neck, the arms and the foot — the grammar goes rigid along with the woman. `reddere motus`, "to give back movements", is how a limb answers an intention. `intra ... viscera saxum est` is the finish of the change: this is not a coating over her, it goes the whole way in.

sentences.t:
Flet tamen. Et validi circumdata turbine venti
in patriam rapta est. Ibi fixa cacumine montis
liquitur, et lacrimas etiam nunc marmora manant.
sentences.l: Still she weeps. And, wrapped round by the whirl of a strong wind, she was snatched away to her native land. There, fixed on a mountain top, she melts, and even now the marble runs with tears.
sentences.i: Still she weeps. Caught up in the whirl of a strong wind, she was carried off to her own country. There, fixed on a mountain top, she melts away, and to this day the marble runs with tears.
sentences.n: `Flet tamen` — two words, after seven lines of everything she can no longer do; weeping is the one thing left, and the sentence is short because there is nothing else in it. `manant` is transitive here: the marble is the subject and the tears are its object, so the stone "runs tears". Her native land is Lydia and Sipylus, the mountain of line 149, so the tale ends where it began. `etiam nunc`, "even now", makes it something a reader could go and look at — the standard closing move of an aetiology, a story told to explain a thing that is still there.
